title: The four Labour Codes: a plain-language map
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Twenty-nine central laws were folded into four Codes. Here is what each one covers.
body:
Parliament passed four Labour Codes in 2019 and 2020, merging 29 central labour laws into four. Anyone who works with labour questions, whether as a union leader, a lawyer, an employer or a worker, should know what each Code is about, which older laws it replaces and why it has been debated so intensely. This post is a plain-language map, not a legal opinion; the text of each Act should be consulted for exact wording.

## How the Codes came about

India's labour laws grew up one at a time over a century. A factory worker, a miner, a dock worker and a journalist were each covered by a separate Act, often with a separate definition of "wages" or "employee". Reformers argued for years that this was confusing and left many workers outside any law. The Codes were the Government's answer: group the laws by subject into four.

The Code on Wages was passed by the Lok Sabha on 30 July 2019 and the Rajya Sabha on 2 August 2019, and received the President's assent on 8 August 2019. The other three Codes were passed by the Lok Sabha on 22 September 2020 and the Rajya Sabha on 23 September 2020, and received assent on 28 September 2020. Labour, as an earlier post explained, is on the Concurrent List, so these are central laws that State governments support with their own rules.

## The four Codes

**Code on Wages, 2019** covers minimum wages, timely payment of wages, bonus and equal remuneration. It replaces four older laws: the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 and the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976. Its notable features include minimum wages for all employees in organised and unorganised sectors, a national floor wage below which State minimums cannot fall, a ban on gender-based pay discrimination and overtime at twice the normal rate. Its "wages" definition counts basic pay, dearness allowance and retaining allowance; other components can make up at most half of total remuneration, and any excess is added back for purposes such as provident fund and gratuity.

**Industrial Relations Code, 2020** covers trade unions, standing orders, lay-off, retrenchment, closure and strikes. It replaces the Trade Unions Act, 1926, the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 and the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Among its provisions: standing orders apply to establishments with 300 or more workers, up from 100; prior government permission for lay-off, retrenchment and closure also applies at 300 workers, up from 100; a union with 51 per cent membership is recognised as the sole negotiating union; a 14-day notice is required before a strike in all establishments; and fixed-term employment is permitted with parity of wages and benefits. A retrenched worker is to receive an amount equal to 15 days' wages into a reskilling fund.

**Code on Social Security, 2020** covers provident fund, ESI, gratuity, maternity benefit and, for the first time, a framework for gig and platform workers. It replaces nine laws, including the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923, the Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948, the Employees' Provident Funds Act, 1952, the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961, the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 and the Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008. It defines aggregators, gig workers and platform workers, and provides that aggregators contribute 1 to 2 per cent of annual turnover, capped at 5 per cent of what they pay to such workers. Fixed-term employees become eligible for gratuity after one year instead of five.

**Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020** covers safety, health and working conditions in factories, mines, docks, building work and other establishments. It replaces 13 laws, among them the Factories Act, 1948, the Mines Act, 1952, the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970, the Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act, 1979 and the Building and Other Construction Workers Act, 1996. It sets an eight-hour day and a 48-hour week as the baseline, requires written appointment letters, replaces six registrations with one, and raises the threshold for the contract labour law from 20 to 50 workers.

## Why one law each?

The older laws had different definitions of "employee", "wages" and "establishment", so the same worker could be covered by one Act and left out of another. The aim of the Codes is uniform definitions, fewer registrations and returns, and wider coverage. The Government's statements at the time claimed, for instance, that the Code on Wages would extend minimum wage protection to the whole labour force, where earlier laws covered a smaller part of it, and the Finance Minister said in 2019 that standardised definitions should reduce disputes.

## Where the debate lies

Supporters see simplification, wider coverage and a first framework for gig workers. Critics, including trade unions, focus on specific provisions. The Industrial Relations Code is the main focus: the higher thresholds for lay-off and closure mean that fewer establishments need government permission to retrench, the strike rules are stricter, and recognition rules decide which union may bargain. Reports on the Code note that a concerted casual leave by more than half of the workers can count as a strike. Thresholds for the contract labour and standing orders laws also determine how many workplaces fall under them. These are the kinds of points on which unions asked for changes.

## BMS's position

BMS has said that it welcomes the simplification and the extension of social security, but has also argued, in consultation with the Government, that some provisions need to change so that workers' rights are not diluted. In its pre-budget submission of January 2025, it asked that the Code on Wages and the Code on Social Security be brought into force and that provisions it considers anti-worker in the other two Codes be removed before their remaining provisions were notified. A 2025 article in *Organiser* describes the position as supporting the progressive parts of the Codes while opposing provisions that restrict union recognition or collective bargaining. BMS's website separately records a meeting with the Labour Minister on the Codes, at which the Government promised amendments, and nationwide protests over long-pending workers' issues and the Codes. Readers should treat these as BMS's account of its own position.

## A later note on enforcement

Passing a law is not the same as bringing it into force. Parts of the Codes were notified in stages. Reports state that the four Codes were brought into force on 21 November 2025, with rules to follow, which is after this post's date. Anyone applying the Codes should therefore check the current notifications on the Ministry of Labour and Employment website, and the State rules, rather than rely on any summary, including this one.

## What remains to be done

Three tasks stand out. First, rules and schemes must give practical meaning to the framework: the gig worker provisions in particular depend on schemes yet to be built. Second, there is the position of workers outside the framework, such as scheme workers who are paid honoraria, whom BMS wants recognised as workers. Third, unions will watch how recognition, strike notice and retrenchment rules work in practice. Later posts will take each Code in turn.
